Broken record: Contested boundaries, founding challenges and a provincial govt dismissed. The issues of Dawn of Aug 18 till Aug 24, 1947 were dominated by the announcement of the Radcliffe Commission award, setting the formal boundaries of the dominions of Pakistan and India, while communal violence, and efforts to quell it on both sides, also featured prominently on the pages. In more welcome news, the bureaucracy in the nascent state rolled up their sleeves to take up the task of nation-building — which remains a work in progress, mind you — while congratulations continued to pour in welcoming Pakistan to the comity of nations. In the Aug 18 edition, the reaction in the lead story to the announcement of the Radcliffe Commission award was highly critical. “The decisions embodied in the reports very materially alter the boundaries as set forth provisionally under the national division and it is the Indian Union which gains all along the line at the expense of Pakistan.” In a related report, Sardar Abdur Rab Nishtar, the Communication Minister, acerbically termed it “a parting kick of the British”. Clearly, the founding fathers felt His Majesty’s government had pulled a fast one on Pakistan. Apparently, they were not wrong. Aug 18’s lead editorial termed Sir Cyril Radcliffe’s decision “Territorial Murder”. As the editorial noted, the decision had come like a “bolt from the blue. They represent the award of only one man, Sir Cyril Radcliffe, the Chairman [of the commission]. … The Muslim nation has been betrayed. … Pakistan has been cheated of large areas in the Punjab, Bengal and the district of Sylhet which … belonged to it.” This was, in the words of the Quaid-i-Azam, a “moth-eaten Pakistan”. Punjab disturbances Communal bloodshed, particularly in Punjab, remained a major concern for both Pakistan and India. As the lead story on Aug 19 noted, there were “widespread massacres in the Eastern Punjab, particularly in the Amritsar district.” So serious were matters that Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan, and his Indian counterpart Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru were briefed on the security situation by Sir Claude Auchinleck, who was supreme commander of both dominions at the time. The Quaid was also informed of the situation by the PM. Taking care of business, UN application But even in the midst of grave challenges, there was much work to be done. As the joy of living in a newly independent nation began to sink in, so did the gravity of the task of governing it. Aug 19 was the first working day of the Pakistan government. The Aug 20 edition noted that “about 5,000 Officers, typists and assistants, turned up for work. All the files have not yet arrived from Delhi.” It added that “every means of conveyance was used” by the public servants of the new state to show up for duty; even “camel carts were not considered too undignified”. Can you imagine today’s babus showing up for work in carts drawn by animals, or even worse, using public transport like the rest of us plebeians? Perish the thought. Nothing but the slickest, most expensive wheels for today’s ‘servants’ of the people. Meanwhile, as the Aug 18 issue reported, Pakistan submitted its application to the United Nations. “The formal letter of application arrived from Karachi at United Nations Headquarters today [Aug 16]. Interestingly, the UN Legal Department had decided that while the “new Dominion of India would continue to be an original member state” of the UN, “Pakistan, as a new State, would have to apply for membership.” Thankfully, Pakistan’s application was accepted in September 1947, with Afghanistan casting the sole vote against this country’s membership. Pakistan greeted In the days after independence, numerous heads of state wrote to the Quaid congratulating Pakistan on its birth. For example US President Harry S. Truman assured Pakistan of the “firm friendship and goodwill of the USA.” French Foreign Minister Georges Bidault described the raising of Pakistan “to the rank of the great free nations as a step of great importance for the whole world.” Al-Haj Amin al-Husseini, Grand Mufti of Jerusalem (which had not yet been occupied by Israel) offered the “most sincere congratulations of your Palestinian brethren and their best wishes.” Haile Selassie, Emperor of Ethiopia, took “great pleasure in extending our greetings” to Pakistan while the Iranian Prime Minister Ahmad Qavam said: “May Pakistan become a great bulwark of freedom, peace and brotherhood in Asia”. Clearly, nations of the East and West had great expectations of Pakistan. Dr Khan Sahib’s ministry The Aug 23 issue contained a news item many current readers will find quite interesting, to say the least. As per a communique issued from Governor House Peshawar on Aug 22, “Dr Khan Sahib’s Ministry has today [Aug 22] been dismissed from office and the Governor has invited Khan Abdul Qayum Khan, Leader of the Opposition Muslim League Party in the NWFP Legislative Assembly to form a Ministry”. Dr Khan Sahib was the brother of Khan Abdul Ghaffar Khan, the “Frontier Gandhi”, who famously did not see eye to eye with Pakistan’s founding fathers. Dr Khan Sahib’s Congress Ministry had taken office in March 1946, and had faced a civil disobedience movement. An elected government in the NWFP (now KP) led by an opposition party was sent home by the centre at the birth of Pakistan. Sound familiar? With the advantage of hindsight, one has the opportunity to study the historical cycles in a nation’s life. Thanks to this newspaper’s unique, extensive archive of back issues, one can examine the major political, economic and social trends that have shaped Pakistan and the world over the last seven decades and counting. Cliched as it may sound, history repeats itself, and we — as a state and as a polity — largely refuse to learn from it. Through this platform, we will look back at the ‘big’ stories that made it to the front pages of Dawn, as well as significant developments tucked away in the inside pages, from the birth of Pakistan onwards, and try to put them in perspective. We will study the critical issues of the week, starting from Aug 14, 1947 and examine the major themes and issues that made it to the paper.

Trump paused Russia sanctions to 'analyse' impact on global economy: Rubio. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Saturday that President Donald Trump’s waiver of sweeping sanctions and tariffs on Russia would be a 60-day pause to “analyse” their impact on the global economy. “The president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy and even to the US economy,” Rubio said, noting that the economic restrictions involved a number of countries, not just Russia. He said various conflicts were impacting global energy prices, including the US war on Iran and attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen’s Houthis. “These conflicts around the world are starting to crash into each other, and they’re having an impact not just on global oil and diesel prices” but on economies as well, Rubio said. Trump said late on Saturday his decision would benefit the US, though it was unclear if he had actually made up his mind on the matter. “We’ll figure it out, and you’ll figure it out,” he said. “It’s a very good decision, and it’s going to be a decision that’s good for the country, and I think good for the world.” US lawmakers on both sides of the political aisle have sharply criticised Trump after he signed an executive order Friday that waived sweeping sanctions and tariffs targeting Russia — measures adopted by Congress last month. The law passed in September, and signed by Trump, included sanctions targeting Russian officials, oligarchs and financial institutions, and provided Trump with the authority to impose sanctions on major buyers of Russian oil and gas. The idea was to cut off sources of funding to supporters of Russian President Vladimir Putin, as well as his war on Ukraine. But late Friday, two days before the law was due to take effect, Trump exempted Russia from those economic restrictions. “Beyond irresponsible,” Republican Senator Thom Tillis, a frequent Trump critic who will leave office in January, said in a post on X. “If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid for Vladimir Putin.” Ted Cruz, a senior Republican senator from Texas, called the move “a mistake” in comments aired on Fox News . Trump’s executive order came after he struck a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to allow exports of Russian diesel in exchange for the easing of sanctions. The impact of steep diesel price hikes due to the Iran war are beginning to filter into the US economy, and cost of living worries are top of mind for voters ahead of key midterm elections next month. Polls show Trump’s Republicans are likely to receive a drubbing at the polls. “The diesel that Putin was going to sell, they were (going to) make it available to the global market one way or the other. The only difference is how much of it the United States was going to get,” Rubio said, underscoring the importance of the vital fuel powering US road hauling, agriculture and construction. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky said he feared the United States would lift more sanctions on Russia and that Trump’s action “rewards” Putin.

Out-of-control truck kills 13 at religious festival in India's Madhya Pradesh. A speeding truck in India killed 13 people when it ploughed into a crowd at a Hindu festival, officials said on Sunday, with President Droupadi Murmu describing the deaths as “heartbreaking”. The heavily loaded truck reportedly lost control in the early hours of Sunday and hit devotees gathered at a temple in Gwalior, in the central state of Madhya Pradesh. The Press Trust of India (PTI) news agency cited hospital officials as saying 13 people had died. “I express my deepest condolences to the bereaved families and pray for the swift recovery of those injured,” Murmu said on social media. The Indian Vice President C.P. Radhakrishnan expressed sorrow at the loss of life. “Deeply saddened by the tragic loss of lives in the accident involving devotees in Gwalior, Madhya Pradesh. My heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families. I wish a speedy recovery to all those injured,” he wrote in a post on X. The incident comes a day after at least 17 people were killed and two dozen more injured on Saturday in eastern India after a stampede that was likely caused by sudden rainfall during a Hindu religious gathering, officials said. India, with 1.4 billion people, recorded more than 183,000 road traffic deaths in 2025, or over 500 a day, according to the roads ministry. Many are linked to inadequate road infrastructure, ill-maintained vehicles and exhausted drivers, according to official data.

'Serious incident' at Canada base causes deaths, sparks fire: govt. Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said late on Saturday there were “fatalities and injuries” following an incident at a military base in western Canada. “I’m saddened to share that there have been both fatalities and injuries as a result of an incident on the base,” identified as Wainwright in Alberta, McGuinty said. Prime Minister Mark Carney had posted to X earlier on Saturday that “a serious incident creating a major fire” had occurred at the base. Neither offered details on the number of casualties or the nature of the incident at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, located about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton. “We will have more to say in the coming hours and days,” McGuinty said. CFB Wainwright is one of the busiest Army bases in Canada. A doctor at a hospital in the city of Edmonton, about 200 km northwest of the base, told public broadcaster CBC that Wainwright’s health-care facilities were “completely overwhelmed” by the number of patients requiring care. “It is more patients than any of us want to count right now,” Warren Thirsk said. “It’s a disaster. It’s a one in every 15 to 25-year disaster.” The Municipal District of Wainwright posted on social media that the fire had “spread rapidly due to high winds.” It said later on Saturday that the blaze was “being held at this time,” though firefighting crews would continue to monitor the area. Carney said the government was working closely with Alberta officials and local authorities. “Our thoughts are with all the brave women and men affected,” he said on X. The fire also disrupted advance voting ahead of Monday’s referendum on a future poll on whether Alberta wants independence from Canada. Alberta’s office responsible for overseeing provincial elections said the advance voting station in Wainwright had closed.

One in three adults in Pakistan lives with psychological disorder: study. KARACHI: Pakistan’s first nationally representative mental health survey has shown that nearly one in three adults is living with a diagnosable mental and behavioural disorder, highlighting a major public health challenge affecting millions of people across the country. The findings come from the largest and most comprehensive mental health study ever conducted in Pakistan, say researchers representing the Pakistan Psychiatric Society (PPS). The five-year research is published in the British Medical Journal . The survey was led by Professor Raza-ur-Rahman from Hamdard University, Karachi, in collaboration with Brighton and Sussex Medical School UK, University of South Florida, US, and psychiatric institutions across Pakistan. Experts term findings of first national mental health survey ‘most reliable’ Nearly 18,000 adults from all four provinces participated in the 2018-2022 study, providing the first nationally representative picture of mental health in the country. Key findings The study found that 32 per cent of adults were currently living with mental and behavioural disorders, while 38 per cent had experienced a disorder during their lifetime. One in five adults met criteria for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD). More than one in 10 adults had depression, whereas six per cent reported suicidal thoughts in the previous month. Researchers also identified significant social inequalities in mental health. Higher rates of mental disorders were found among older adults, individuals with lower levels of education and income, unemployed people, and those who were widowed, divorced or separated. Mental health problems were associated with substantial impairment in family life, social relationships and the ability to work. “This survey provides the evidence needed to develop effective mental health policies and services in Pakistan. It identifies who is most at risk, where support is most needed, and the scale of the unmet need for care,” said lead investigator Prof Raza-ur-Rahman, currently heading the department of psychiatry at HU. According to him, the researchers used international standard tools to carry out the survey and the Pakistan Bureau of Statistics identified the areas for survey and provided the sample size. He hoped that it would contribute to reducing stigma and improving access to diagnosis and treatment for millions of people. “For the first time, policymakers, healthcare planners and researchers now have reliable national data that can be used to strengthen mental health services, allocate resources more effectively and develop evidence-based programmes across the country,” he added. The study represents a major milestone for mental health research in Pakistan and demonstrates the country’s growing capacity to undertake large-scale, internationally recognised public health research. Prof Anjum Memon, Chair in Epidemiology and Public Health Medicine at Brighton and Sussex Medical School (UK) and the senior co-author of the study, said: “This is a landmark moment for mental health research in Pakistan. For decades, policymakers have had to rely on fragmented local studies or international estimates. We now have robust national evidence showing, for the first time, the true scale of mental and behavioural disorders across the country.” These findings provide an invaluable evidence base for policymakers, clinicians and healthcare planners, not only in Pakistan but also in other low- and middle-income countries facing similar challenges, he added. Mental health, researchers say, is increasingly recognised as an essential component of national health and economic development and they recommend greater integration of mental health services into primary healthcare, increased investment in community-based support systems, enhanced training for frontline health workers and sustained national efforts to reduce the stigma surrounding mental illness. “Pakistan currently faces major challenges in the provision of mental healthcare, including limited specialist services and a shortage of trained mental health professionals. The survey findings will help inform future policy development, service planning, workforce training and community-based support programmes,” said President of PPS Prof Wajid Akhundzada. Japan to launch historic round-trip mission to Mars moon. Japanese scientists are preparing a mission to Mars’s moons to retrieve samples that could help unlock the origins of the solar system and life on Earth, in what aims to be the first round trip to the Martian region. The unmanned Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) probe, a collaboration with US and European space agencies as well as numerous universities and tech companies, could also help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration. The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX is set to blast off from the Tanegashima Space Centre on Tuesday at 4:41 am (12:41am PKT), according to the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). The spacecraft will arrive near Mars one year later, where it will orbit its moon Phobos for up to three years before landing and collecting at least 10 grams (0.35 ounces) of material from the surface. A rover dubbed IDEFIX — the French name for the comic hero Asterix’s dog — will first conduct surface observations aimed at ensuring a safe landing. “The sampling (from) Phobos is of course the world’s first, but it means… this is the first round trip to the Martian system,” MMX’s project manager Yasuhiro Kawakatsu told AFP . JAXA said the mission will also explore the possibility of using Phobos as a “natural space station” by establishing the requirements for a round trip to Mars — something “essential for crewed Mars exploration”. It will also observe the Red Planet’s moon Deimos, although it will not land on it, before returning to Earth. Impact or capture JAXA hopes the mission will reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, a key piece of knowledge in working out how the Solar System was born. One theory for the origin of the Martian moons — the “giant impact” hypothesis — is that they formed after a celestial body collided with Mars. The “capture” hypothesis, meanwhile, postulates that the moons are asteroids captured by Mars’s gravity. Determining which is right will help reveal “how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets”, JAXA said, referring to the four rocky worlds closest to the Sun — Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars. “MMX will shed light on the transport mechanisms that delivered water, volatiles, and organic compounds from the outer solar system to the inner rocky planet region — processes that may have played a key role in making these worlds habitable,” said Patrick Michel, a French astrophysicist working on IDEFIX. “If Phobos and Deimos are indeed remnants of these early delivery systems, they may hold clues to the origins of life itself, or, to be more correct, to the transport of the materials that were key to the emergence of life on rocky planets,” he told AFP . Deep in the ‘gravity well’ MMX is a collaboration with France’s National Centre for Space Studies (CNES), the German Aerospace Centre (DLR), Nasa, the European Space Agency (ESA), and about 20 universities and tech companies. The development of the spacecraft’s landing legs was particularly difficult, as gravity on Phobos is extremely weak, JAXA scientists say. Japan’s unmanned Smart Lander for Investigating Moon (SLIM) — the “Moon Sniper” — tipped over after touching down on Earth’s Moon in 2024, but still transmitted data and survived several two-week lunar nights. Japan also has experience in bringing back samples from space, including JAXA’s unmanned Hayabusa-2, which returned 5.4 grams of rock and dust collected from an asteroid several hundred million kilometres from Earth in 2020. One of the differences between JAXA’s past asteroid probes and the MMX mission is that this time “we have to travel very close to Mars and return”, which means escaping the planet’s heavy gravity, Kawakatsu told reporters. Phobos orbits about 6,000 kilometres above the Martian surface. “Going deep into what we call the ‘gravity well’ is difficult,” Kawakatsu said. China’s mission US and Chinese space agencies have been racing to be the first to return rock samples from Mars’s surface back to Earth. Nasa’s Perseverance rover , which has been roaming the Red Planet since 2021, has already collected samples. The mission, however, was effectively cancelled by the administration of President Donald Trump following a vote by the US Congress in January. China, meanwhile, has announced its Tianwen-3 spacecraft is scheduled for launch around 2028 and hopes to return Mars samples to Earth as early as 2031 — potentially before the MMX’s return. JAXA scientists say sand and rocks from Phobos may offer a wider variety of samples than those on the planet itself, especially if it was formed by a collision between a celestial body and Mars.

Ram Leela Temple in Dera Ismail Khan sealed amid demolition fears. DERA ISMAIL KHAN: The authorities here on Saturday locked and sealed the historic Ram Leela Temple in Rahim Bazaar days after civil society activists intervened to stop the demolition of the heritage building for the construction of a commercial plaza at the site. The building had earlier been sealed by Assistant Commissioner Hamid Siddiq following public protests and work at the site was stopped, said local sources. The latest development came as civil society representatives and members of the Hindu community held a joint meeting to discuss the reported move to demolish the temple. The participants condemned the proposed construction and called on elected representatives to raise the issue in the National Assembly. The meeting, held at the office of civil society president Sohail Ahmed Azmi, was attended by former MPA and Hindu community representative Kishore Kumar, social worker Muhammad Nauman and others. The participants said the Ram Leela Temple was among around 400 buildings in Dera Ismail Khan identified as cultural heritage properties by the Evacuee Trust Property Board. They expressed concern over any move to demolish the temple and said civil society, the business community, writers and heritage advocates would resist any action that could damage the city’s historical heritage. The participants also alleged that the relevant authorities had allowed construction of a commercial plaza at the site despite questions over their legal authority to do so. They called for an inquiry into the matter and said complaints would be submitted to the district administration, the NA speaker, the archaeology department and other relevant authorities. Digging in Karachi for Red Line damages gas pipeline, disrupts supply. KARACHI: Gas supply to several areas of the metropolis was suspended during lunch hours on Saturday after a high-pressure pipeline was damaged during excavation work for the Bus Rapid Transit (BRT) Red Line on University Road, adding to the miseries of residents in the affected areas. The disruption affected Gulshan-i-Iqbal, areas around Mazar-i-Quaid, parts of Garden, Saddar, Burns Road and several other localities. A spokesperson for the Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) said that the high-pressure pipeline near the Gulshan-i-Iqbal telephone exchange on University Road was damaged at around 1pm during BRT construction activity. She said teams immediately reached the site and started repair work, which was completed by 5pm. “After completion of the work, gas supply was restored,” she said. Residents in the affected areas said the sudden suspension caused considerable inconvenience, particularly during cooking hours. Several households reported disruption in preparing afternoon meals, while commercial eateries and roadside hotels in Saddar and Garden saw a rush of customers as many people had no option but to dine out or take food home for their families. Domestic consumers complained that low pressure persisted even after the announced restoration time. Many families said they had to arrange food from nearby restaurants. “We had guests at home and the gas suddenly disappeared. We had to order biryani from a nearby hotel, which cost us extra besides causing embarrassment,” said Rozina Adnan, a resident of Saddar. Another resident from Garden said his wife could not cook and they had to bring food from a restaurant for the children. Published in Dawn, October 18th, 2026

Pakistan suspends Iran trade corridors over 'security, smuggling concerns'. GWADAR/QUETTA: Pakistan has suspended trade with Iran through the official Gabd-Rimdan (250) and Taftan border crossings, it emerged on Saturday. The Ministry of Commerce issued a memorandum on Friday, seen by Dawn , withdrawing its earlier order [No. 9(3)2017-Iran] dated Oct 3 with immediate effect. Shahid Rind, adviser to the Balochistan chief minister on media and political affairs, said the “purpose of the temporary closure of the Pak-Iran border is to address security concerns, prevent smuggling, and make the border system more effective”. In a statement on X, Rind refuted “rumours being spread on social media” regarding the closure and urged the public not to pay attention to unverified information. The Balochistan official stressed that the move was “necessary to improve the security situation and administrative affairs on both sides of the border”. Rind affirmed that “progress continues between the high officials of both countries to resolve administrative issues” related to the border. “In the context of the current progress, the Pak-Iran border is likely to reopen soon,” he said, adding that a coordinated system was being established to improve border affairs and prevent smuggling. Meanwhile, Iran’s foreign ministry spokesperson Esmail Baqaei also said the closure was temporary, Iran’s state-run Irna reported . However, he attributed the move to “technical issues” and said the two countries were in consultations to resolve the problem and restore normal operations. Separately, the Quetta Chamber of Commerce and Industry (QCCI) has also advised its members and businesses involved in trade with Iran to stop placing new import and export orders until further notice. Hundreds of freight vehicles carrying liquefied petroleum gas (LPG), rice, fresh fruit and other essential commodities have reportedly been stranded on both sides of the border. According to Iran-based Wana news agency, passenger traffic through the Rimdan–Gabd crossing remains operational. It quoted Syed Hossein Hosseini, director general of the Iranian Transit Office, as saying that commercial operations at the border crossing had been halted. The Gabd-Rimdan crossing had become a major route for meeting Pakistan’s energy needs, with over 4,000 tonnes of LPG reportedly imported daily through it. Exports of Pakistani products, particularly rice, had also surged in recent months, generating millions of dollars in foreign exchange. Sources in the trade and energy sector warned that the closure could aggravate LPG shortages in Karachi and other parts of the country. The Taftan route was already facing disruptions amid unrest in Balochistan. The suspension of supplies through Gabd-Rimdan could push up LPG prices in the open market. Local traders and the chamber have warned that the disruption could cause not only substantial losses to the national exchequer and jeopardise the livelihoods of many but also an energy crisis. Since March this year, Islamabad and Tehran have rolled out a series of measures to facilitate border trade, including easing customs procedures , formalising Taftan as a customs station, and notifying new transit routes , against the backdrop of the ongoing US-Iran war that has strained economies in the region and beyond. In early August, an Iranian delegation led by Trade and Industry Minister Mohammad Atabak visited Islamabad for the 10th session of the Pak–Iran Joint Trade Committee (JTC). The delegation also met with Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, with both sides agreeing to further expand trade ties by keeping border crossings open round the clock, improving logistics and harmonising customs procedures. The visit came a couple of months after it was reported that trade between Pakistan and Iran through the Gabd-Rimdan border crossing had come to a complete halt. According to Gwadar Chamber of Commerce and Industry President Jiand Hoot, trade through the Panjgur and Mand-Radig border crossings was virtually non-existent because of poor road infrastructure and recurring incidents of arson and vehicle burnings.

Saudi-led coalition says 2 pilots killed in helicopter crash near Yemen. The Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis on Sunday said two pilots were killed when their helicopter crashed near the Yemen border, after the group claimed it shot the aircraft down. The coalition blamed a “technical malfunction” for the incident, which inflicted its first military fatalities since the long-running conflict with the Houthis reignited in July. The incident comes a week after strikes by the Houthis killed 13 people at Riyadh’s international airport, the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. “An AH-6i reconnaissance helicopter belonging to the Ministry of National Guard crashed inside Saudi territory in Najran Region due to a technical malfunction,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Malki said, according to the official Saudi Press Agency . “The accident resulted in the martyrdom of its aircrew, consisting of two officers.” Late on Saturday, Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed the group had “downed an Apache helicopter belonging to the Saudi enemy” in the same area. After an uneasy, four-year truce, Yemen’s conflict has surged back to life and intensified when the group seized strategic territory along the Red Sea coast last month. The Houthis have hit Saudi targets including tankers in the Red Sea , oil facilities and Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport . The Saudi-led coalition backing the internationally recognised government has launched repeated air raids on Houthi territory. The coalition said overnight that it intercepted two drones in the Riyadh area and a third over the oil-rich Eastern Province. Saudi authorities had earlier issued a threat alert in the capital. Two ballistic missiles “launched by the terrorist Houthi militia towards Khamis Mushait” were intercepted in the kingdom’s south, the coalition added. On Saturday, the Houthis reported that Saudi strikes killed 12 people in Yemen, including three children. The Houthis have declared a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia and captured territory around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, the Red Sea chokepoint and vital export route for Saudi oil since Iran blockaded the Gulf’s Strait of Hormuz. On Sunday, Egypt’s parliament will hold an emergency session after President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi asked lawmakers to authorise support to defend Saudi Arabia against Houthi attacks. Sisi said he was willing to “carry out any measure to protect” Saudi Arabia if its leaders requested it. “I’m not talking about fighting anyone or attacking anyone,” he said on Saturday. “We are speaking only about defence.”

8 India-sponsored terrorists killed in Quetta, Khuzdar, Nushki districts: ISPR. Security forces have killed eight “India-sponsored” terrorists during three intelligence-based operations conducted in the Quetta, Nushki and Khuzdar districts of Balochistan, Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) said on Sunday. The IBOs took place on Oct 17 (Saturday) on the “reported presence of terrorists belonging to Indian proxy Fitna al Hindustan ”, the military’s media affairs wing said in its press release . The state has designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna al Hindustan to highlight India’s role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. In the Panjpai area of Quetta district, terrorists’ attempt to establish a roadblock to disrupt local traffic was “intercepted by security forces, resulting in [the] killing of five India-sponsored terrorists”. Separately, during a sanitisation operation in Nushki district, security forces busted a terrorist hideout and “after an intense fire exchange, two India-sponsored terrorists were sent to hell”. Weapons and ammunition were also recovered, ISPR added. In another IBO in Khuzdar, a terrorist hideout was “engaged by security forces through prompt offensive action”, killing one terrorist. ISPR said a large quantity of explosives (490 kilogrammes) was also recovered. Sanitisation operations were being conducted to eliminate any other terrorist found in the area, according to the statement. ISPR reaffirmed that the “relentless counterterrorism campaign under Vision ‘ Azm-i-Istehkam ’ (as approved by the Federal Apex Committee on the National Action Plan) by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and supported terrorism from the country”. President Asif Ali Zardari, in a statement, paid tribute to the security forces for eliminating eight terrorists. He also commended their professional capabilities for thwarting the attempt to disrupt traffic in Quetta, as well as their actions in Nushki and Khuzdar. “Conspiracies of the terrorists’ foreign patrons and their local facilitators will be foiled,” President Zardari declared. Intensified operations Balochistan has witnessed an increase in terrorist activities in recent years, prompting security forces to intensify counterterrorism operations. On the night of Oct 12/13, security forces busted a terrorist hideout and killed five terrorists during an IBO in Washuk, ISPR said . Days later, Balochistan government officials said that six terrorists affiliated with the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP), two would-be female suicide bombers, and two commanders of a banned organisation had been arrested during IBOs across the province. They said around 90 arrested terrorists were being held at a centre where investigations and legal proceedings were under way. Earlier this month, five terrorists were eliminated in Balochistan’s Mastung district, state media reported . The number of terrorist attacks in the province increased by seven per cent from 83 in July to 89 in August , according to data compiled by the Pakistan Institute for Conflict and Security Studies (PICSS). As per the report, Balochistan was declared the province “most affected” by terrorism.

What is holding up the US-India trade deal?. United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to visit India for the second time this year, as Washington seeks to bolster ties with a strategic partner despite months of friction over a trade deal. Rubio will meet senior Indian officials, but will bypass the Indian capital during the trip in the coming week. Instead he will focus on investment and energy during visits to financial hub Mumbai and India’s oil hub of Jamnagar, which is home to billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s refining complex, the world’s largest. The elephant in the room will be the inability by both countries to seal their long-awaited trade deal , experts say. Several factors, including US President Donald Trump’s tariff blitz, friction over energy imports and Washington’s warmer ties with India’s arch-rival Pakistan have made it harder for negotiators to clinch an agreement. Rubio will start his six-day overseas trip on Saturday with a visit first to Uzbekistan before arriving in India, according to the US State Department. Here are some of the challenges the trade pact has faced and the road ahead. Why has the deal been delayed? India and the United States agreed in February on the framework for an interim deal under which Washington would lower reciprocal tariffs from 25 per cent to 18pc and India would reduce duties on a range of industrial and agricultural goods. Despite months of negotiations, the agreement has not yet been finalised and signed. One reason is the legal uncertainty surrounding Trump’s tariff plans after court challenges undermined the reciprocal tariffs that formed their basis. “The February framework had offered to reduce India’s reciprocal tariff… in return for substantial Indian concessions. Once that tariff regime was struck down, the value of the US offer became unclear,” trade expert Ajay Srivastava said in a note. India is also wary of new trade measures by Washington that could impact it, including an investigation into alleged unfair practices in several countries and a new law that allows for up to 100pc tariffs on nations that purchase Russian oil. Trump on Friday signed an executive order that waived those threatened sanctions. Where do negotiations stand? Progress appears to have hit several hurdles. For the better part of this year, both governments spoke optimistically about the possibility of finalising the interim deal. US ambassador to India Sergio Gor in June said negotiators were working on the “last one per cent” of the pact. More recently, the tone has turned markedly cautious. India’s Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said last week that talks had hit a “plateau”, with little room for further concessions. Her remarks came days after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said an announcement was not “imminent”. What have been the main sticking points? Agriculture remains a sensitive area for India, which is reluctant to expose farmers to greater foreign competition. Washington, meanwhile, wants India to buy more US energy supplies. New Delhi has also insisted that its final tariff rate should be competitive with those received by other regional manufacturing rivals such as Vietnam. Indian trade minister Piyush Goyal said this week that the first tranche of the deal was in its final stages, but added that it would not be operational until India secured an edge over its competitors. “It’s going through the final contours, the legal drafting, and we hope to be able to finalise that soon and operationalise that once we get competitive advantage over our peer countries,” he said. How has trade been holding up? Goods exports to the US jumped 21pc in August to $8.3 billion compared to the same month a year earlier, when India faced 50pc tariffs. The surge in exports has been a bright spot for the Indian economy, which has been roiled by high energy prices due to war in the Middle East. If higher tariffs were to return, economists say it would cast a shadow on India’s growth outlook, hurt market sentiment and heap pressure on an already-weak rupee.

Musk back in the spotlight, but politics dims the awe. With a sports car that somersaults through the air, Elon Musk is back in the headlines for technological daring — but his plunge into politics and his return to US President Donald Trump’s side mean the world’s richest man no longer enjoys the unqualified praise of years past. “All the things that we were promised since the 1950s, of space travel and flying cars… he’s doing all of those things,” said Andrew Selepak, a social media professor at the University of Florida. “And yet we’re not giving it the attention, we’re not giving it the awe that it probably truly deserves,” he added. In recent weeks, Musk has seemed to be everywhere at once. On Sept 28, SpaceX’s Starship megarocket reached orbit for the first time and deployed 26 Starlink satellites before splashing down in the Pacific — a milestone for the rocket central to Musk’s Mars ambitions. Musk’s central role in geopolitics has also been on display, with Ukraine complaining of disruptions to the Starshield satellite communications system its military relies on. Even the platform formerly known as Twitter is enjoying something of a renaissance, with Musk’s X now the go-to social media app for Silicon Valley insiders and the main marketplace for talk about artificial intelligence. But despite his continued success, Musk’s unrelenting commitment to right-wing politics has taken a toll. No image captured that shift more than Musk brandishing a chainsaw on stage in February 2025 — a gift from Argentine President Javier Milei — as a symbol of his drive to slash the US government as head of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) in the early months of Trump’s second term. Through DOGE, Musk’s allies fanned out across federal agencies, driving cuts that effectively dismantled the US Agency for International Development (USAID) and contributed to a net loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs. ‘National treasure’ That combative imagery has been matched by Musk’s posts on X, where hardline anti-immigration views and right-wing conspiracy theories sit alongside posts about rocket launches and Tesla robotaxis. Now Musk is back in Trump’s good graces, after a spectacular falling-out that followed his exit from DOGE in May 2025. Last week, Trump presented Musk with the nation’s top science medal, calling him a “national treasure” and “our modern-day Thomas Edison”. The renewed relationship comes as Musk has spent at least $276 million on Republican political campaigns ahead of next month’s midterm elections, in which the president’s party is expected to struggle. Of that, $158m is funding a massive advertising campaign in Texas, Musk’s home state, where the Republican candidate is trailing in the polls. US President Donald Trump presents the National Medal of Science to Elon Musk during the “Golden Age of American Innovation Summit” at the Institute of Peace in Washington, DC, on Oct 8, 2026. —AFP/File For left-leaning pundits, Musk is now increasingly seen as an agent of Trump and the tech billionaires rather than a technology savant working for the good of humanity. That opposition plays out in ‘Musk’, a four-hour documentary by Oscar-winning filmmaker Alex Gibney now in US theatres, which traces the life and career of the South Africa-born billionaire. “I once described him as somebody who can jump off the edge of a cliff and invent a parachute on the way down. I think he thrives on chaos,” Musk’s first wife Justine Musk, who features prominently in the film, told podcaster Kara Swisher. Yet, she added, “I always assume that there’s a method to his madness,” and many of his loudest actions may in fact be deflections and “sleight of hand”. The same may be true of Musk’s dealings with Washington. Few entrepreneurs depend as heavily on the federal government as Musk does. SpaceX — which went public in June in the largest initial public offering in history — earns billions of dollars a year from Nasa and Pentagon contracts, while Tesla’s bet on robotaxis hinges on how quickly regulators allow driverless cars onto US roads. Seen in that light, Musk’s millions for Republicans may be less a political conversion than an investment.

First Pakistani astronaut to undertake space mission from China on Nov 25: Ahsan Iqbal. Pakistan’s first astronaut will undertake a space mission from a Chinese space centre on November 25, Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal said on Sunday. The minister made the announcement while addressing the concluding ceremony of World Space Week in Narowal, held in collaboration with the Pakistan Space and Upper Atmosphere Research Commission (Suparco), the planning ministry said in a statement. According to the handout, the planning minister also said the country was aiming to achieve a lunar landing by 2035, expressing hope that Pakistan’s cooperation with China would help it “reach new heights in space exploration”. In his address at the ceremony, the planning minister highlighted the importance of space technology in agriculture, communications, climate monitoring, education and national security. Iqbal stressed that scientific research and space exploration were essential for technological advancement, the ministry’s statement said. He further noted that Muslim scholars had once made significant contributions to astronomy and scientific discovery, calling for renewed efforts to restore Pakistan’s leadership in knowledge and research. The astronaut will be one of the two — pilots Zeeshan Ali and Khur­ram Daud— China selected in April this year as candidates for its manned space programme and who have been undergoing intensive training in Beijing. China has not said which of the two will fly or when, but speaking to Reuters last month, Amer Gilani, who oversees human spaceflight cooperation at Suparco, said a final astronaut selection decision was expected in mid-to-late October. According to another Suparco official quoted by Reuters , once in space, the chosen pilot will carry the title of “payload specialist”, which is astronaut-speak for someone whose job in orbit is running Pakis­tan’s science experiments rather than flying the ship. The astronaut will fly aboard a Chinese-built spacecraft, launched from a Chinese site, trained by Chinese instructors and communicating in Mandarin in orbit.

PM Shehbaz inaugurates Daanish School in Islamabad, stresses equal academic opportunities. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif on Sunday inaugurated a Daanish School in Islamabad, saying the initiative aimed to provide quality education to talented students from underprivileged backgrounds and give them opportunities equal to those available to children from affluent families. Daanish schools, originally introduced by the Punjab government , aim to provide quality education to marginalised and talented students. It is said to be the largest network of boarding schools for girls and boys in the country. Speaking at the inauguration ceremony today in the capital today, the premier highlighted stories of Daanish School graduates, including a girl from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa who overcame challenges and a woman from Bahawalpur who went on to become a doctor after losing her father in childhood. “Ladies and gentlemen, this was a vision we had seen in Punjab when I was its servant. How come the sons of rich people enter the iron steel gates of Aitchison College; sons of prime ministers, governors, bureaucrats, judges, civil servants, military servants, landlords, mill owners, regardless of their acumen and their level of intelligence,” PM Shehbaz said. “And those millions of boys and girls, [who are] extremely intelligent, but come from the poorest of backgrounds in the four corners of Pakistan, Azad Kashmir and Gilgit-Baltistan, cannot even imagine opening the gates of Aitchison College, let alone having the opportunity to receive a decent education,” he noted. According to the premier, this vision led his team to establish Danish Schools back in 2010. “[The] concept was introduced in Punjab, not only to match the quality and level of Aitchison College and other grammar schools all over Punjab and other parts of Pakistan, but to excel,” he asserted. PM Shehbaz stressed that every child deserved equal opportunities, whether they were the son or daughter of the richest man in Pakistan, the prime minister or anyone from the elite class, or a child who had lost both parents. “If these children are left to waste their time in the muddy streets of their villages and cities, then this is not the Pakistan of Quaid-i-Azam Muhammad Ali Jinnah. This is certainly not his Pakistan,” he remarked. The premier noted that the richest people in the country, regardless of how they earned their wealth, had the opportunity to send their children to the best schools in Pakistan and even to North America and the south of France. “Imagine the plight of children like this daughter from Bahawalpur, this daughter from KP, and this boy sitting before you, who also became a doctor.” A post by the Prime Minister’s Office (PMO) said, “A new dawn of education and excellence is about to rise in the capital!” PM Shehbaz also interacted with multiple students at the campus. Education Minister Khalid Maqbool Siddiqui also spoke on the occasion. The foundation of the school in the federal capital was laid in 2024, with 10 acres of land allocated by the Capital Development Authority. In March, thousands of students across Pakistan sought admission to the school, which received over 7,000 applications against just 210 seats. The school’s board of governors had also approved a budget of Rs3.8 billion for the year 2026-27 earlier this year.

President of Maldives to visit Pakistan for 3 days at PM's invitation: FO. Maldivian President Dr Mohamed Muizzu will undertake a three-day state visit to Pakistan from Oct 20-22 at the invitation of Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, the Foreign Office (FO) said on Sunday. President Muizzu will be accompanied by First Lady Sajidha Mohamed and a “high-level delegation comprising cabinet ministers and senior officials”, according to a statement issued by the FO. During the visit, the Maldivian president will meet President Asif Ali Zardari, who will host a state banquet in his honour, the statement said. He will also hold “restricted and delegation-level” talks with PM Shehbaz, it added, noting that in these talks, the two leaders “will review the entire spectrum of bilateral relations and explore avenues for further strengthening cooperation in trade, investment, health, education, tourism, agriculture, defence, maritime security, climate change and people-to-people exchanges”. They will also exchange views on regional and international developments of mutual interest, the FO added. A Pakistan-Maldives Business Forum will also be held during the visit to promote interaction between the two countries’ business communities and explore opportunities for trade and investment, according to the FO. “A number of agreements and Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) covering diverse areas of bilateral cooperation are expected to be signed during the visit,” the statement added. The FO highlighted that the visit marks the first by a Maldivian president to Pakistan in 11 years. It will take place as the two countries mark the 60th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1966. “Pakistan and Maldives enjoy warm and fraternal relations rooted in shared faith, mutual respect, longstanding goodwill and close cooperation at regional and international forums,” the statement said. The forthcoming visit reflected the “shared commitment of both countries to further strengthening their bilateral partnership and opening new avenues of mutually beneficial cooperation”, it added. In 2015 , former Maldivian president Abdulla Yameen Abdul Gayoom undertook a two-day state visit to Pakistan on May 6-7 at the invitation of then-premier Nawaz Sharif. He was scheduled to visit earlier that year, but the trip did not materialise.

My father survived the Karsaz bombing; each new terror attack takes us back there. This piece was originally published on June 1, 2022. Over the last few decades, there is a severe burden of ‘resilience’ that has been thrust upon the inhabitants of some large cities in Pakistan, whether it is in the form of persistent rates of crime, diseased public utilities, unbreathable air, floundering healthcare or dismal transportation infrastructure. This oft-romanticised resilience is once more being demanded by the state as citizens of cities like Karachi, Quetta and Peshawar are again being pushed into an unhappy reunion with an affliction that has reared its ugly head after a relative lull — accelerating terror attacks at home. Deadly incidents of this nature are cause for serious emotional instability among residents of these cities. But by now, many locals have whittled down emotional survival to a fairly simple and linear process: Internal security event → temporary panic and lament of said event → desensitisation → next internal security event → repeat. It may seem somewhat callous to reduce this to such a mechanical progression, but the defence mechanisms adopted by those who live in the midst of frequent terrorism are not really up for judgment. If sanity is to be preserved, some form of detachment is necessary. And as someone who has personally employed this process many times in the past, I can say that it works, and works well at that. Until your father is present at the site of a bombing. Then the process comes crashing down. When calamity hits home Karachi, 18th October 2007: Celebrations of Benazir Bhutto’s return to Pakistan were met with two bombs ripping through Karsaz in quick succession, killing nearly 200 people and injuring 500 others. Jammers were activated, emergency was declared, and public healthcare facilities were put on high alert. My father was drowning somewhere in this sea of deadly chaos. The rest of us were home when the news found us. On hearing it, my mother lost all sensation in her legs and collapsed. We began dialling my father’s mobile phone number but couldn’t get through because of the jammers. There was no way of knowing if he was safe, or injured, or even alive. The only information we could get was coming from our television set — all I remember of it now is a crimson BREAKING NEWS template designed to incite fear and a casualty count that was escalating with horrifying frequency. We kept dialling my father’s number desperately in the hope that we could break through the infrastructural blockade imposed by the state. The minutes kept passing and panic kept mounting. At this point, there is no formula or process in the world that can help you. You’d think crying would come naturally at this time but it doesn’t; you are too gripped by fear to respond as you normally would. Your heart throbs and you lose basic bodily control. You are gasping for air and trembling all over, and it is a Herculean task to collect yourself enough to focus on dialling a number, over and over again. As soon as they could, my father’s brothers and cousins set off to find him — I vaguely remember one of them rushing into the car without his shoes on. They didn’t think about what would happen if another bomb went off in a city that appeared to be under the control of terrorists. Frankly, I don’t think they cared. The meaning of family truly comes through in times of crisis, and if there’s one thing to be grateful for in a society where relationships are unravelling constantly, it is to have the support of loved ones who prioritise those bonds above all else. But that’s a subject for another time. Hurt is good Soon after they left, we received a phone call from my mother’s sister in Hyderabad. She had somehow miraculously gotten through to him. “He’s hurt,” she told us. How hurt, she could not say — she had only spoken to him for a few seconds. In the days that passed, we would come to learn that shrapnel from the bomb had pierced through his torso and legs, lodging pieces of metal deep inside his body and permanently damaging a large part of his intestinal tract. But at that time, ‘he’s hurt’ was good to hear. We were happy with hurt because hurt meant alive, and alive meant hope. My father had found his way to an ambulance that was taking him to the Jinnah Postgraduate Medical Centre — a designated hospital for injuries and casualties — but he eventually ended up at (what is now known as) the Dr Ruth Pfau Civil Hospital Karachi. The cosmic irony of the situation is still astounding — at the time, my father was employed at the Civil Hospital as Professor of Surgery. Had any patient in his condition come to the hospital that night, they would have been surgically operated on by my father and his team. And yet here he was, bleeding profusely out of his abdomen, playing the role of patient instead of surgeon. As word spread through the hospital that one of their own was injured, a team of healthcare workers began stabilising him for surgery. He was operated on at around dawn, some hours after hell exploded in Karsaz. My father lost half his intestines that morning in a procedure known as a hemicolectomy. He was in intensive care for the weeks that followed. Metal still remains lodged in his body, buried deep in his bones. But he is with us today. Words cannot express how grateful we are for this, and all of us pray constantly for his sustained health. The scars that never heal Words can, however, attempt to convey the depth of trauma we were exposed to as a family that night, and the lasting impact it has had. Nearly 15 years later, I have still not been able to talk about it. I can only write about the horror of October 18th, protected by the façade of screens and the comfort of one-way communication. If the bombing comes up in conversation, I change the topic; when I fail at that, I leave the room. That period of my life haunts me completely and is triggered every time there is a terror attack in Pakistan, especially in my hometown Karachi. As one can imagine, it has been particularly difficult to deal with the spate of IED bombings in Karachi these past few months. Nights have been spent with tears, terror, and trauma as memories of 2007 find their way into bedtime thoughts and nightmares. There is little hope for stability that can be offered by a leadership that is forever dancing with these forces of terror, sometimes in negotiation and at other times in battle with them. Loss of innocent life remains an unrelenting theme in Pakistan. The mental health impact of living with terrorism day in and day out remains an invisible cost that goes unfactored and uncared for. We are mentally breaking down inside. But so long as we appear functional on the surface, who really cares about what’s going on internally? Some among us are still able to deal with terrorism using the standard emotional survival process mentioned at the beginning of this piece. My own emotional response, unfortunately, has changed. It now goes: Internal security event → terror → incapacitation → next internal security event → repeat. Header illustration: Panuwach/ Shutterstock.com
