Niger Wrestles with the Aftermath of a Military Revolt mloukili Thu, 10/08/2026 - 16:13 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Nigerien soldiers participating in a rally in support of General Abdourahamane Tiani (not seen) outside the former National Assembly in Niamey, on 2 September, 2026. AFP. Q&A / Africa 08 October 2026 11 minutes Niger Wrestles with the Aftermath of a Military Revolt A mutiny by Niger’s special forces in late August morphed into a coup attempt. In this Q&A, Crisis Group experts explain how the unrest exposed growing discontent within the military’s ranks. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Related Tags Niger What is happening? Niger’s military leadership continues to reel from a coup attempt that exposed serious divides within the defence and security forces. On 28-29 August, soldiers from Niger’s Special Forces began shooting in their barracks at Air Base 101, which lies within the compound of Niamey’s international airport and houses most of the country’s military aircraft, as well as army units and foreign troops. Unrest quickly spread: groups of soldiers attacked the state broadcaster and the presidential palace, both in the city centre. Whether the incident began as a mutiny or whether it was meant from the start to oust General Abdourahamane Tiani, who seized power in a July 2023 coup, remains unclear. But the ramification of an uprising by a group of well-trained soldiers unhappy with their conditions of service and recent battlefield setbacks could be significant – particularly if it deepens divisions within the armed forces and disrupts their operations at a time when jihadist threats are looming large across several parts of the country. Members of the Special Reconnaissance Battalion for Special Operations Command, known by the French acronym BSR-COS, appear to have been behind the coup attempt, although a small number of soldiers from other units may have joined. Loyalist forces, particularly the presidential guard that Tiani commanded from 2011 to 2023, fought back as gunfire and detonations shook the capital, while national radio and television temporarily stopped broadcasting. By midday on 29 August, the mutineers withdrew to Air Base 101, where they unsuccessfully sought to rally other units to join them in toppling the government. Their stand did not last long, however. By the evening, national TV was up and running again, broadcasting images of loyalist forces arresting dozens, including at least one female soldier. A few days later, the government organised a national funeral for three members of the presidential guard forces who died in the clashes, while media reported that at least 27 mutineers were killed. The clashes further unsettled civilians in the capital, where heavy gunfire and explosions had already jolted residents twice this year, in January and June, when jihadists attacked the international airport, leaving many increasingly anxious about their safety. Why did the soldiers rebel? Tensions had been building within the BSR-COS for some time. In the days leading up to the revolt some soldiers had reportedly refused to go on a mission, citing a lack of adequate equipment. The battalion’s commander, Major Boubacar Maïhatchi, was detained soon after in the town of Tera as he returned from a mission escorting supply trucks from neighbouring Burkina Faso. Social media platforms have portrayed Maïhatchi as popular among younger officers, who respect his bravery and concern for his troops. His arrest may have prompted the soldiers’ decision to turn against the military leadership. The BSR-COS is part of Niger’s elite special forces, trained and equipped to work specifically in high-danger zones. As jihadist violence intensified in western Niger starting in the mid-2010s, the government expanded these forces, creating additional battalions, often with training and equipment from Western partners such as the U.S., France, and Germany. Today, there are more than a dozen battalions of roughly 500 to 600 soldiers each. The BSR-COS is among the most recently established units, with its members receiving training in Morocco. These battalions are leading the fight against jihadist insurgencies in Niger, including Islamic State Sahel Province and Jama’ at Nusratul Islam wal Muslimin (JNIM) in the west. From its headquarters at Air Base 101, the BSR-COS has frequently assisted units under attack from jihadists or escorted convoys travelling through dangerous areas. In November 2025, for instance, Niger sent 82 fuel tankers to Mali to ease shortages caused by a JNIM blockade on the city. Members of the battalion led the military escort that protected the vehicles during the 1,400 km journey. While special forces battalions are valuable to the fight against jihadists, they are also capable of posing a serious threat to the military regime. Since winning independence from France in 1960, Niger has experienced five coups and several failed coup attempts. The army has long held sway in politics. Seven of its eleven presidents have been military officers. Given that history, Niger’s leaders are understandably wary of powerful military units. Where to deploy the special forces often presents the authorities with a dilemma. As the jihadist threat draws closer to the capital, their presence is increasingly indispensable to protect strategic localities and sites. At the same time, their proximity to the seat of power also fuels concerns within the military regime about the risk of yet another coup. The BSR-COS was initially expected to deploy to Ayorou, a jihadist hotspot near the Malian border where the government is building a large dam crucial for electricity and irrigation. That deployment was delayed in part because of militant attacks on Air Base 101 in January and again in June 2026. Why are soldiers unhappy with Niger’s top military leaders? The incident revealed a widening gap between the military leadership and the rank and file. The July 2023 coup brought senior officers from various components of the defence and security forces to power, ranging from the presidential guard and the army to the gendarmerie and the national guard. Together, these senior figures formed the National Council for Safeguarding the Homeland, which shapes government policy and military strategy. Four generals wielded the most influence in the council: Abdourahmane Tiani, who had himself sworn in for a five-year presidential term in 2025; Defence Minister Salifou Mody, his second-in-command; Mohamed Toumba, who heads the interior and security ministry; and armed forces chief of staff Moussa Salao Barmou, who has since been removed. Yet beneath the military brass that had seized control of the country, discontent has been simmering in the lower ranks. The senior officers justified their power grab partly by accusing the civilian government they toppled of failing to tackle the jihadist threat. Three years on, insecurity has grown and spread to more parts of the country; the opening of new fronts has stretched the defence and security forces thin. Troops are deployed to the front line more frequently and remain there longer. Foot soldiers complain that they lack adequate weapons and equipment. They allege air or ground reinforcements are slow to arrive when needed, if they arrive at all. Combat vehicles and pickup trucks are often in poor shape and the government has been slow to replace them, which makes working in high-risk zones hazardous. Conditions in military barracks have added to soldiers’ frustrations. Some have posted images on social media of the poor-quality meals they are served; others pool their money and buy condiments to improve their rations. On top of that, a recent wave of jihadist attacks – in Diffa, Dosso, Tillabery and Niamey – has killed dozens, draining troop morale. Senior command seems aware of the rumblings. The defence minister, the chief of army staff and other generals have made multiple visits to military bases to listen to soldiers’ concerns. They often blame sanctions imposed by foreign powers after the July 2023 coup for hampering their ability to procure arms. Most of these sanctions have since been lifted, however, and many soldiers appear unconvinced by the senior leadership’s explanation for the lack of equipment. In several instances soldiers’ frustration has manifested in defiance. The August revolt was Niger’s fourth episode of military unrest in less than two years. In June 2025, after an attack in Banibangou in northern Tillabery killed over 70 military personnel, soldiers assigned to retake the position protested and beat the officer in charge, who was later evacuated for medical treatment. A few days later, soldiers in the Zinder region mutinied and tried to kill their superior. In August 2025, soldiers in Ayorou rebelled and opened fire on their commander. As one officer puts it, “A mutiny is first and foremost a failure of leadership”. What did the coup attempt and its aftermath reveal about military divisions? The incident broke an unwritten rule that has long guided Niger’s military: namely, it is essential to avoid internal confrontations between different branches of the armed forces. In 2023, various military units opposed Tiani’s move to detain then-President Mohamed Bazoum in order to remove him from office, but senior commanders ultimately decided to avert an open conflict and rally behind Tiani’s power grab. This time around, the mutineers fought the presidential guard, while the government asked Russia’s Africa Corps to help quell the revolt. Hours after the August revolt had subsided, Russia’s ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropayev, told reporters that Russian forces had helped subdue the dissidents. Around 200 men from Africa Corps, the expeditionary force controlled by Russia’s defence ministry, have been deployed in Niger, including at Air Base 101, since 2024. They have assisted the regime with intelligence gathering, training on drone use, and operating air-defence systems. Russian forces reportedly used kamikaze drones that explode upon impact to force the mutineers to surrender. Some within the military found the involvement of foreigners in an internal confrontation particularly grating. Rumours have it that armed forces chief of staff Barmou may have been among those who voiced reservations about the Africa Corps’ intervention against the mutineers. In any event, on 11 September Tiani replaced Barmou with General Mamane Sani Kiaou, a move observers interpreted as aimed at reasserting control over the army. Barmou was also among the first generation of Nigerien special forces officers trained by the U.S. in the 2000s; he had reportedly threatened to resign previously over the army’s lack of equipment and his limited influence over military decision-making. Regime authorities, meanwhile, arrested over a hundred soldiers, while dozens of others, including special forces members, remain unaccounted for. Several civilians were also arrested, including two former ministers and a prominent journalist. The coup attempt could accentuate the resentment many troops feel vis-à-vis the presidential guard. The elite unit has long had access to the best equipment and the most talented recruits. It also foiled several coup attempts in the 2010s and early 2020s, leading some in the armed forces to perceive the guard as preoccupied with policing the military and protecting the regime rather than national security. Finally, the failed coup demonstrated that public support for the military regime is declining. The generals’ promises to restore security, overhaul governance, and assert Niger’s sovereignty on the international stage won a degree of sympathy from the public early on. But much of that enthusiasm has evaporated amid repeated security setbacks and an economic slowdown, partly attributable to the departure of Western donors and the closing of many NGOs by the government. On the afternoon of the coup attempt, regime supporters called on Niamey residents to turn out in support of the military leadership; notably, only a few dozen people did so. How did the incident reverberate in the region? The unrest had major diplomatic repercussions. The following day, a Nigerien officer speaking on national television alleged that he had received calls and messages from contacts in Chad, France, Belgium and the United Arab Emirates (UAE), informing him that several foreign countries – including Chad, Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and France – were prepared to intervene in support of those who had seized Air Base 101. He said they were operating with the blessing of the Economic Community of West Africa, the regional bloc from which Niger – alongside Burkina Faso and Mali – withdrew in 2025. On 3 September, the government spokesperson accused France of orchestrating the mutiny and alleged that “other African countries” had supported Paris. Some of these accusations were unsurprising. Tiani has repeatedly accused Benin, Côte d’Ivoire and France of conspiring against him, allegations the countries have rejected. But the regime’s claims that Chad was somehow also intent on destabilising Niger were new. Niger’s relations with Chad have soured in recent months. Niger’s authorities and their counterparts in Chad have traded accusations of tolerating, or even supporting, armed opposition groups active in their common border zones. Chadian officials did not respond to the allegations, although President Mahamat Idriss Déby later posted Quranic verse on social media warning against mixing truth with falsehoods. At the same time, the failed coup brought northern neighbour Algeria closer to the Nigerien authorities. Algeria condemned the incident and sent its chief of army staff to Niamey along with four fighter jets and a refuelling aircraft. The deployment of the fighter jets was apparently aimed at sending a strong message of support and to deter any attempt by foreign interests to dislodge the regime. The gesture also reinforced a diplomatic thaw already under way between the two countries. Relations had deteriorated last year after Algeria shot down a Malian drone near its border, prompting Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger – the three members of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) – to recall their ambassadors from Algiers. Niger and Algeria have since taken several steps toward rapprochement, culminating in President Tiani’s visit to Algiers in February. The episode has also reinforced Niger’s relationship with Russia. Moscow’s intervention demonstrated the growing importance of Russian security support to the authorities in Niamey. In turn, the episode could deepen the regime’s dependence on Moscow for its survival. Since the coup, most Western forces have left Niger, including U.S. and French troops, as well as German, Belgian and Canadian personnel involved in training the Nigerien armed forces. Today, only a few hundred Italian troops remain, making Italy the last Western country with a military presence in Niger. What should the authorities do next? The Nigerien authorities should exercise restraint during their ongoing post-coup crackdown. While those within the BSR-COS who instigated the mutiny will likely face sanctions, the authorities should spare the rank and file who simply followed commanders’ orders. Thus far, over a hundred soldiers have been arrested. A sweeping purge risks further weakening the armed forces, deepening mistrust between ranks and damaging troop morale at a time when Niger is under enormous pressure from jihadists and rebel groups. Restraint will not address the grievances that helped fuel the revolt, however. The authorities should tackle soldiers’ concerns about inadequate equipment, housing and food. A leaked 2020 defence audit exposed widespread corruption in procurement practices. In February 2024, however, Niger’s military authorities issued an ordinance exempting defence and security procurement from ordinary state contracting and public accounting oversight. Without compromising legitimate security concerns, the authorities could adopt a stronger approach to rooting out wrongdoing in the acquisition of military equipment, as well as improve living conditions in the barracks. The authorities should also tread carefully in order not to deepen divisions between different wings of the defence and security forces. Even symbolic decisions matter. The national funeral held for three presidential guard soldiers reinforced perceptions of double standards: regular soldiers who are killed in the line of duty are often buried quietly and rarely honoured publicly. A more equitable recognition of soldiers’ sacrifices could help reduce resentment across the ranks. More fundamentally, Niamey needs to reduce the mounting burden on its armed forces. The authorities should develop a comprehensive strategy for dealing with the proliferation of conflict fronts, giving greater weight to non-military approaches. Where possible, dialogue and diplomacy could help pacify restive areas. Even if such approaches do not produce sustainable peace, they could help demobilise combatants, achieve temporary ceasefires, and possibly reduce the number of simultaneous conflicts, providing relief to armed forces that show growing signs of fatigue. Finally, the authorities should recognise that military discontent is unfolding in an increasingly closed political environment. With political parties dissolved and civic space severely restricted, peaceful avenues for expressing dissatisfaction with the government have narrowed considerably. In such an environment, the armed forces risk becoming one of the few remaining channels through which opposition to the regime can erupt, and potentially in its most dangerous form. Reopening political and civic space would allow grievances to be expressed through less destabilising channels, even if doing so exposes the authorities to greater public criticism. On Our Radar eschelhaas Fri, 10/09/2026 - 00:00 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Special Coverage / Global 09 October 2026 20+ minutes On Our Radar On Our Radar scans conflicts and crises around the globe every week and features some of the hotspots Crisis Group’s analysts are closely watching. Whether an under-reported trend or a headline-grabbing development, our field experts explain why it matters or what should be done. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print 9 October 2026 HAITI Haiti’s electoral council announced changes to the country’s voting rules Tuesday. The new law, which will likely result in delays to polls presently scheduled for 13 December, will remove provisions that would have disqualified individuals subject to bilateral sanctions imposed by third countries from running for office. Those subject to UN sanctions remain barred from candidacy. The move comes as the UN Panel of Experts on Haiti, which makes private recommendations to the Security Council regarding who should be sanctioned, denounced several high-profile politicians for using gangs to fuel violence. Some UN Security Council members worry that sanctioning public figures could interfere with Haiti’s political process. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the risk of inaction is greater, however: those who have collaborated with gangs could return to power, further delaying resolution of the Haitian conflict. MALI On Tuesday, the Malian army recaptured Kidal, a strategically important city in the country’s north that had been held by the separatist Front for the Liberation of Azawad (FLA) since April. The FLA said it had decided to temporarily withdraw from Kidal as the army, backed by Russian Africa Corps paramilitaries, launched a large-scale offensive. Crisis Group expert Ibrahim Maïga says the recapture of Kidal is a significant military development. But without a political process to build on these gains, the takeover alone is unlikely to bring this conflict closer to a lasting resolution. UKRAINE A Russian attack on Kramatorsk in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region killed at least 33 people on a public bus Thursday. Previous Russian strikes across the country Wednesday killed at least 28 others, including 22 when a missile hit a residential building. Kramatorsk – one of the cities Russia has been unable to capture in Donetsk – has become an important supply hub for the Ukrainian army. The attack came as Kyiv struck a data centre belonging to Russia’s largest technology company, Yandex, in the central Ryazan region, south east of Moscow. Crisis Group expert Lucian Kim says both sides are using long-range strikes to put pressure on their adversaries, though Russia’s aerial campaign is far more devastating, raising the number of casualties among the civilian population and upending daily life for millions. 2 October 2026 MYANMAR Military airstrikes on a market in Kyauktaw, Rakhine State, on Monday reportedly killed at least 50 people. The UN described the attack as one of the deadliest in the state since the 2021 coup. The Arakan Army, an ethnic Rakhine group, vowed on Tuesday to take “retaliatory measures” against those responsible. The strikes came amid a military counter-offensive launched in early September on several fronts in and around Rakhine to retake territory from the Arakan Army. It has made little headway, says Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean. The market raid was likely intended to punish civilians and disrupt trade and governance in Arakan Army-held areas of Rakhine. U.S. - IRAN U.S. and Iranian negotiators held indirect talks on the UN General Assembly’s sidelines to end a conflict now in its eighth month. On 26 September, U.S. President Donald Trump said he had rejected an Iranian ceasefire proposal but continued to make counteroffers. On Wednesday, Trump warned of further military action, saying: “We blow them up or make a deal”. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says prospects for a breakthrough appear slim: Tehran proposes reopening the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for the U.S. lifting its blockade of Iranian ports and releasing Iranian assets. Washington believes it has overcome Iran’s efforts to restrict shipping while continuing to weaken the Iranian economy. Tehran also wants to defer nuclear issues to subsequent talks; Washington seeks concessions up front. Fear of escalation could keep the door to engagement open, but significant gaps over substance and sequencing remain. YEMEN Fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces and their allies intensified this week, including around Taiz, a city in the middle of the country, where the rebels have been seeking to cut the road link with Aden on the southern coast. Taiz is home to more than 2 million people, many of whom have been displaced from other parts of Yemen. Meanwhile, the World Health Organization warned that Yemen’s health system was nearing “breaking point” amid mounting casualties. Crisis Group expert Ahmed Nagi says Houthi success around Taiz could help consolidate the group’s gains along the Red Sea coast. Diplomacy faces substantial obstacles: the Houthis are unlikely to accept de-escalation without tangible concessions from Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s government, while Riyadh may seek limited battlefield gains before mediation. 25 September 2026 SOUTH SUDAN President Salva Kiir dissolved South Sudan’s transitional unity government Tuesday, three months before elections scheduled for 22 December, dismantling key power-sharing institutions established under the 2018 peace agreement. Following a hurriedly passed amendment to the National Elections Act, Kiir dismissed all five vice presidents, including his long-time rival First Vice President Riek Machar, and installed a caretaker government composed entirely of loyalists. Crisis Group expert Daniel Akech says the changes allow Kiir to concentrate authority in his hands. Greater control of state institutions could help him retain power, through either a stage-managed election or a delay that prolongs his administration. The resulting political exclusion risks provoking greater conflict in an already deeply fractured country. UNITED NATIONS World leaders met this week in New York for the UN General Assembly’s annual high-level session. Crisis Group expert Daniel Forti says the week’s events proved that states still value the UN as a forum for discussing global concerns, even if common ground between them remains elusive. Some countries expect the next Secretary-General to single-handedly get the UN back on track and provide solutions for crises around the world. That attitude is short-sighted. The UN needs the conviction of its members to tackle global risks from deadly conflict to artificial intelligence. Whether states choose to work together – or continue down the path of international fragmentation – will determine whether the next decade at the UN is defined by diplomacy or disorder. U.S. - CHINA President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a state visit in Washington this week. Xi touted their personal rapport, called for “healthy” bilateral competition “within bounds” and argued that U.S.-China cooperation is needed to address most global challenges. Crisis Group expert Ali Wyne says the summit’s outcome was modest: the two leaders agreed to extend by two months the trade truce that they blessed in Busan, South Korea last October; it was due to expire on 10 November. They do not appear to have made a breakthrough on managing cross-strait ties, spurring diplomacy to end the U.S.-Iran war or erecting guardrails around artificial intelligence. China’s readout called on the U.S. to “adhere to the correct position of opposing ‘Taiwan independence’”, incorrectly but provocatively implying that the U.S. had changed its longstanding position (that it “does not support” that outcome). 18 September 2026 DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO Protesters streamed into the streets of Kinshasa Tuesday to decry the government’s proposals to change the constitution by popular referendum. One person was killed in clashes with police who intervened to stop the marchers from reaching parliament. Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff says the government’s main aim in trying to alter the constitution is to revise the clause imposing a two-term limit on presidents, thereby allowing the incumbent Félix Tshisekedi to stand for a third term. Tshisekedi is keen to hold the referendum soon, despite the opposition, because he senses that the country’s political balance has tilted in his favour. Going ahead with this vote may prove unwise, however, even if it comes off fairly smoothly. It may produce an illusion of political stability that, in turn, deflects attention from urgent tasks like reducing poverty among ordinary Congolese and taming the interlinked wars raging in the eastern provinces. MALI Algerian Prime Minister Sifi Ghrieb visited Bamako Monday in the latest sign of rapprochement between Algeria and Mali, whose relations had deteriorated badly in recent years. Crisis Group expert Jean-Hervé Jezequel says the thaw is welcome news for the Malian authorities. Bamako has been struggling to contain an insurgency linked to al-Qaeda, Jamaat Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), which killed 50 Malian soldiers in its latest attack on an army base last week. JNIM has lately allied with northern separatists who have also been fighting the Malian army. Historically, Algiers has been an important mediator between Bamako and northern armed groups. The warming of Algeria-Mali relations raises hopes that it might again play such a role, though maybe a more limited one given the Malian authorities’ increasingly sovereignist mindset. It could nevertheless help mitigate the conflict that has torn at Mali since 2012. PHILIPPINES Regional parliamentary elections took place on Monday in the Bangsamoro, the swathe of the southern Philippines that won autonomy in 2019 as part of a 2014 peace agreement between Manila and the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF). At least five people were killed and twenty injured during the vote, though violence was less widespread than feared, with incidents concentrated in a few locations. No party secured an absolute majority, meaning that politicians will likely need to form a coalition. Crisis Group expert Georgi Engelbrecht says the incoming government, slated for inauguration by 30 October, will likely pair former MILF rebels with representatives of the region’s traditional political clans, unless the ex-insurgents, who have split into two factions, can reunite. The elections were a big step forward for the Bangsamoro peace process, with all eyes now on a crucial meeting between national government and MILF delegations to discuss gaps in fulfilling the 2014 accord’s terms. 11 September 2026 IRAN The International Atomic Energy Agency referred Iran to the UN Security Council Wednesday for breaching its nuclear non-proliferation obligations, marking the first time in twenty years the organisation has taken such a step. Tehran condemned the decision, blaming U.S. and Israeli strikes on its nuclear facilities for disrupting the agency’s inspections. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says concerns about Iran’s lacklustre cooperation with the UN watchdog have been mounting for years, capped by over a year of blocked access to key sites bombed by the U.S. and Israel in June 2025. Given that UN sanctions were already reinstated last year, and the expectation that China and Russia will shield it from additional punitive measures at the Security Council, the referral may harden Iran’s obduracy rather than cajole it into overdue cooperation. LEBANON Israel stepped up its attacks in southern Lebanon over the weekend with strikes that killed nearly 30 people and wounded dozens more. While Israel claimed that it had targeted Hizbollah arms caches and military installations, the assaults killed several children and medical staff. Crisis Group expert David Wood says Israel’s lethal escalation could continue, unless it faces strong pressure from the U.S., its most important ally, to desist. Washington sponsored a Lebanon-Israel ceasefire struck in late June but, over two months later, the deal remains largely unfulfilled, with Israeli military action continuing and Hizbollah refusing to disarm. SOMALIA Somali piracy has seen an uptick this year, with at least six hijackings of cargo ships and smaller vessels since April. The turmoil resulting from the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran has created opportune conditions for pirates, with fewer naval patrols off the Somali coast and more commercial traffic in nearby waters as ships are diverted from the Bab al-Mandab and the Strait of Hormuz. Crisis Group expert Omar Mahmood says the number of pirate attacks is far below what it was during the heyday of Red Sea piracy fifteen years ago. The current trajectory is concerning, however, and more raids are bound to occur, absent international and local measures both offshore and on land to combat the phenomenon. 4 September 2026 HAITI Armed gang members stormed the commune of Kenscoff, overlooking Port-au-Prince, overnight on 23-24 August, killing at least 47 people and abducting more than 50, whom they threatened to kill if security forces go after the gang in that area. At least thirteen abductees have subsequently been released. Briefing the UN Security Council on 28 August, UN envoy Carlos Ruiz Massieu said the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) would beef up its presence in the capital, while Haitian units would send reinforcements to Kenscoff. Crisis Group expert Diego Da Rin says the Kenscoff massacre is the latest indication that gangs are on the offensive as the GSF assembles. U.S. - IRAN After a month-long lull, the U.S. resumed attacks on Iranian soil over the weekend, first striking rocket launchers on Larak island that Washington said were preparing to deploy sea mines, then hitting dozens of military targets along Iran’s southern coast. Tehran responded with missile and drone fire at bases hosting U.S. forces in the Gulf. Crisis Group expert Naysan Rafati says the uptick comes as the Trump administration tries to isolate Tehran financially through increased sanctions and a naval blockade, while in parallel undermining Iranian efforts to control the Strait of Hormuz by escorting vessels through the waterway. While Washington's approach is to squeeze wherever possible and strike whenever it deems necessary – for example, in response to Iranian strikes or efforts to rebuild its military capabilities – the Islamic Republic could counter with additional strikes of its own on U.S. assets and allies, along with further attacks on shipping. THAILAND Overnight on 22 August, militants in Thailand’s three southernmost provinces staged over 50 attacks in four hours, including bombings and arson attempts at local administrative offices, shops and other buildings. Three passersby were injured. Further incidents followed on 23 and 29 August despite tightened security. Authorities blamed Barisan Revolusi Nasional Patani Melayu (Patani-Malay National Revolutionary Front, BRN), which has fought Bangkok’s rule since 2004. It was likely intended to discredit the state, demonstrate insurgents’ reach and heighten pressure on the government to resume peace talks that have occurred intermittently since 2013. Thailand’s chief negotiator has reportedly proposed bringing technical-level talks with BRN forward from October to this month, in part to determine the reasons for the attacks. 21 August 2026 CHINA - SOUTH KOREA Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi paid a two-day visit to South Korea this week to discuss bilateral ties, Korean peninsula tensions and broader Asian affairs. Crisis Group expert William Yang says the U.S.-South Korean friction has given Beijing an opening to deepen its own engagement with Seoul. SOMALIA Local paramilitaries clashed with federal forces Monday in Baidoa, capital of Southwest state, leaving 30 dead, according to the Somali government. The militia is loyal to Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed “Lafta-Gareen”, a former state president whom Mogadishu forcibly removed in March after a disagreement over state elections. Calm has since returned to Baidoa, but absent an initiative to address lingering grievances over the political transition in Southwest state, further violence is likely. 14 August 2026 IRAN - U.S. Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis attacked a merchant vessel Tuesday near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, killing six people aboard, as the U.S. fired two missiles at a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman to enforce its renewed blockade of Iran-bound maritime traffic. SUDAN The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and allied militias made rapid gains in Blue Nile state this week, taking Geissan town from the Sudanese army Tuesday and advancing into Kurmuk town Wednesday. The RSF appeared to use Ethiopian territory to launch the attacks on the two towns, both of which sit along the border with Ethiopia. Crisis Group expert Alan Boswell says the latest clashes will further drive up tensions between Sudan’s army and Addis Ababa, which accuse each other of supporting their domestic foes. WEST BANK Israeli settlers accompanied by soldiers besieged Palestinians in homes near the village of Qusra Sunday, among them Palestinians with U.S. citizenship. Only after four days and under U.S. pressure did the Israeli army intervene – not to chase away the settlers, but to remove a number of the Palestinians. The government is grabbing land, not only to create facts on the ground that will be hard for any successor to reverse, but to drive Palestinians into isolated, shrinking enclaves. 7 August 2026 CEUTA More than a hundred people died last week when Moroccan authorities apparently loosened controls along the border with Ceuta, a Spanish-administered enclave at the north-eastern tip of Morocco on the Strait of Gibraltar, unleashing an unprecedented rush of would-be emigrants into the territory. Most of those who perished were trying to swim or wade around coastal breakwaters. Following a swift Spanish military deployment, the vast majority of those who entered were returned or voluntarily went back to Morocco within days. Migrant testimony and video footage suggests that Moroccan security services helped facilitate the influx, says Crisis Group expert Riccardo Fabiani. They have previously used the spectre of unregulated migration to strong-arm Madrid into supporting Rabat’s claim to Western Sahara. Why they would use it this time is unclear. A few possible explanations come to mind: to impress upon Spain that its claim to Ceuta (which Morocco disputes) is hard to defend; to remind Madrid that it needs Rabat to protect its interests; and to earn credit with two allies, Israel and the U.S., with which the Spanish government has been at odds over Gaza and the war with Iran. CHAD The Chadian government filed a letter with the UN in late July declaring its intent to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC). It is the fourth African country to take this step since 2025, after Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger. All have cited perceived anti-African bias, pointing to the fact that most of the ICC’s recent probes have focused on African countries. Many, however, will see it as a way to curry favour with Washington to secure its help in counter-terrorism efforts around Lake Chad. Still others – especially among the Zaghawa ethnic group – may espy a government attempt to escape international scrutiny for complicity in crimes in neighbouring Sudan. N’djamena is accused of allowing the United Arab Emirates to funnel arms to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, who have massacred Zaghawa and others in Darfur. ETHIOPIA Hundreds of people have fled into Sudan after clashes last weekend in Shererina, a western district of Ethiopia’s northernmost Tigray province. The fighting flared up along the Ethiopia-Sudan border between the Ethiopian army and forces loyal to the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF). It quickly subsided, but not before raising fears of renewed open hostilities between these two sides, which fought a bloody war from 2020 to 2022. Nevertheless, the border confrontation shows how dangerous the standoff has become. 24 July 2026 THAILAND Militants attacked a checkpoint in Narathiwat, a province on the Malaysian border, on Wednesday, killing four paramilitaries, known as rangers, and an army senior non-commissioned officer. The army’s chief of staff, General Chaiyapruek Duangpraphat, used unusually strong language afterward, saying, “I will have my men hunt [the perpetrators] down in every village and forested mountain area. Crisis Group expert Matt Wheeler says attacks are routine in the country’s deep south, which has been troubled by an insurgency since 2004. These incidents rarely grab national attention, but this one is distinctive for the high death toll and the popular anger excited by widely viewed video footage of what happened. But in the meantime Washington should lift the blockade so as not to create a humanitarian crisis in the pursuit of its goals, and avoid any further escalation. IRAN One month on, the 17 June memorandum of understanding that was to halt hostilities between the U.S. and Iran looks moribund. U.S. forces have been conducting near-daily strikes in Iran throughout the past week and resumed their blockade of Iranian shipping, while Iran has been firing drones and missiles at U.S. bases around the Gulf and in Jordan. LEBANON An Israeli airstrike Thursday killed two people in southern Lebanon, despite negotiations in Rome to end the conflict between Israel and Hizbollah. The latter rejects the Israeli-Lebanese talks, arguing that Lebanon should instead rely on the group’s patron, Iran, to secure a genuine ceasefire and Israeli troop withdrawal as part of a broader deal with the U.S. This position notwithstanding, Hizbollah has largely halted its own military operations in recent weeks. CHINA China test-fired a long-range ballistic missile from a nuclear-powered submarine in the South Pacific Monday, its first such exercise in these waters in two years. Chad said the border would remain closed until further notice, while allowing humanitarian exemptions, including for refugees and returnees, as well as approved aid deliveries. Crisis Group expert Charles Bouëssel says N’Djamena should maintain vital cross-border aid and preserve trade that sustains displaced populations. It should also ensure that security and disarmament operations in the east are conducted with restraint and impartiality to contain intercommunal tensions and prevent Chad from being drawn further into Sudan’s war. CUBA Cuban authorities Wednesday accused ten people on a U.S.-registered speedboat carrying weapons and tactical gear of attempting infiltration of Cuban territory with “terrorist intentions”. Border guards shot four people dead and wounded six others aboard the boat after its occupants allegedly opened fire. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio denied any U.S. involvement and said Washington would investigate the facts independently. Crisis Group expert Renata Segura says the incident comes amid already high tensions between Havana and Washington, after the U.S. halted fuel imports coming into Cuba, exacerbating a severe energy crisis on the island, in hopes of pushing the Cuban authorities to negotiate an economic and political opening. SYRIA ISIS released an audio statement last weekend denouncing Syria’s interim government and calling for a renewed campaign against its forces. The jihadist group has since claimed responsibility for several attacks on Syrian army personnel in the northern and north-eastern parts of the country. These developments follow last month’s reported mass escape from the al-Hol camp, which held over 20,000 detainees, many of them relatives of suspected ISIS fighters. Some of these people got away as security broke down during an offensive led by Damascus on the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF). Crisis Group expert Nanar Hawach says the closure of the camp compounds an already risky convergence. With the SDF sidelined, U.S. forces withdrawing from Syria and the new government’s security apparatus still finding its feet, ISIS seems to be seeking an opening to resume its insurgency. 20 February 2026 MATERNAL MORTALITY The World Health Organization released a study Tuesday showing that nearly two thirds of maternal deaths worldwide occur in countries wracked by conflict or instability. Crisis raises the risks associated with pregnancy, the report finds, though health services in conflict-affected places are generally already scarce. Some countries, such as Colombia and Ethiopia, have made progress in reducing maternal mortality through partnerships with NGOs with expertise in service provision in remote areas. But now aid cuts have put such programs in jeopardy, says Crisis Group expert Cristal Downing, even as women are dying in childbirth at alarming rates. Donor funds still available should be directed toward bolstering community-based health services, particularly in war zones, through such cost-effective means as midwifery. NIGERIA The Nigerian government announced Tuesday that the U.S. will dispatch 100 additional military personnel to assist in fighting jihadist groups in the northern part of the country. This deployment comes amid deadly attacks that killed 56 people in Niger state last weekend and 34 others in Kebbi state on Wednesday. These raids are part of a broader surge of violence that has claimed over 250 lives across north-central and north-western Nigeria in the past month. Hundreds more people have been abducted. Crisis Group expert Nnamdi Obasi says jihadists and other armed groups are growing stronger in these regions and elsewhere, by exploiting gaps in rural and border security as government forces become increasingly overstretched. The U.S. aid notwithstanding, the government needs to urgently improve its response, including by expediting measures outlined under the “nationwide security emergency” President Bola Tinubu declared last November. U.S. - IRAN Iranian and U.S. delegations convened in Geneva Tuesday for talks about Tehran’s nuclear program, the second round of such negotiations this month. In parallel, the Islamic Republic’s foreign minister met with the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency for technical discussions. Both Iran and the U.S. noted a measure of progress, as did the Omani mediators, even as Washington continues to ramp up its deployment of military assets to the Middle East. But the gaps between the sides are still wide, says Crisis Group expert Ali Vaez, even as regards what a possible agreement would cover. The negotiators have yet to wrestle with matters of substance. Tehran and Washington are aware of the high risks of failure, as well as the costs that fresh hostilities would bring. Yet the pace of diplomacy is lagging as momentum builds for confrontation. 13 February 2026 BANGLADESH The Bangladesh Nationalist Party won a landslide victory Thursday in the country’s first national elections since the 2024 ouster of former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, whose Awami League was barred from contesting the vote. A concurrent referendum on the July Charter – a set of reforms negotiated by all the participating parties over the last year – passed by a wide margin. Crisis Group expert Thomas Kean says the turnout and referendum result reflect the credibility of both the election and the reform process in the eyes of most Bangladeshis. The incoming government will face daunting challenges, however, such as getting Bangladesh’s ailing economy back on track and improving security. ERITREA-ETHIOPIA Addis Ababa accused Eritrea of deploying its troops into Ethiopian territory Saturday to conduct joint manoeuvres with Ethiopian rebels along the border. In response, Asmara said Ethiopia had fabricated evidence for this charge, asserting that it has “no appetite for or desire to engage in meaningless acrimony”. Crisis Group expert Magnus Taylor says this latest confrontation comes shortly after renewed clashes between Ethiopia and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front’s armed wing, which Addis Ababa alleges has formed a secret pact with Eritrea. More fighting could be in the offing if efforts to de-escalate tensions fail. WEST BANK Israel’s security cabinet Sunday approved measures that further cement Israeli control of the occupied West Bank, with the explicit goal of pre-empting the establishment of a viable Palestinian state. The move reflects an Israeli plan not only to annex all the Israeli settlements in the rural West Bank, but also to further limit what is left of nominal Palestinian autonomy and displace Palestinians from more built-up areas. Absent action that conditions trade and aid to Israel on policy changes, says Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein, international support for a two-state solution increasingly rings hollow. The annexation drive also undermines the Trump administration’s twenty-point plan for Gaza. 6 February 2026 GAZA Israel carried out strikes across the Gaza Strip Wednesday, killing at least 24 Palestinians. The Israeli army claimed it was targeting a Hamas commander and responding to fire upon its troops, but civilians accounted for most of the casualties. The death toll among Palestinians in Gaza since the October 2025 ceasefire has now topped 550. Humanitarian needs also remain acute amid aid shortfalls; the Rafah crossing with Egypt has opened, after a long wait, but deliveries are still tightly restricted. Crisis Group expert Mairav Zonszein says the latest violence underscores how tenuous the ceasefire remains despite formally entering its second phase, when the sides are supposed to begin addressing issues of long-term security, governance and reconstruction. Islamabad accuses the Afghan Taliban of harbouring the BLA high command, which they also say gets financial and logistical assistance from Pakistan’s arch-rival India. Crisis Group Executive Vice President Richard Atwood says the high death toll among the Baloch separatist insurgents shows that authorities planned the raids carefully, with a view to keeping civilians out of the crossfire. U.S. - COLOMBIA Presidents Donald Trump and Gustavo Petro met at the White House Tuesday after months of heated rhetoric prompted by disputes over issues such as migration, counter-narcotics cooperation and the 3 January U.S. raid grabbing Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro. Amid these exchanges, Trump went so far as to suggest that Colombia, too, might be a target of U.S. military action. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting proved constructive, helping ease the tensions in the bilateral relationship and signalling that the two countries can continue working together to curb drug trafficking. The two presidents also discussed the tariff spat between Colombia and Ecuador, with Trump offering to mediate between these countries’ leaders. Resolving the immediate trade crisis could pave the way for stronger collaboration between Bogotá and Quito in fighting organised crime. 30 January 2026 COLOMBIA - ECUADOR The foreign ministers of Colombia and Ecuador met in Panama after a week in which a trade dispute escalated between the two countries. Colombia retaliated with tariffs on Ecuadorian goods and a suspension of electricity exports. Ecuador then raised the fee for Colombian oil shipped through its pipelines tenfold from about $3 to $30 per barrel. Crisis Group expert Glaeldys González Calanche says the meeting indicates that the two capitals understand the dispute will hurt both economies as well as weaken both states’ ability to confront security challenges on the frontier. Rather than acting in isolation, the two should mount a coordinated cross-border response, which is likely to be more effective in fighting transnational criminal networks. IRAN U.S. President Donald Trump told Iran Wednesday that it risks "major destruction" if it fails to negotiate a nuclear deal with Washington. The ultimatum follows earlier warnings of U.S. intervention over the Islamic Republic's repression of protests. The U.S. has dispatched additional naval assets, airpower and defensive systems to the Middle East. Tehran – along with some of its non-state allies in the region – has threatened retaliation if attacked. The Congolese army and allied Wazalendo militias re-entered Uvira this week, but in the interim chaos engulfed the town, with widespread looting and abuses against civilians, mainly by the Wazalendo. Of particular concern, says Crisis Group expert Richard Moncrieff, is the mounting ethnic tension in the area. The M23 insurgents, who portray themselves as defenders of the Tutsi people, took Uvira claiming that the Tutsi-related Banyamulenge living in town needed their protection. Primary responsibility for attacks on Banyamulenge residents lies with the Congolese authorities and their allies, but the rebels appear to have exposed these people to predictable retaliation after retreating.
